issues.legal_issue: The existence of a Hindu joint family does not by itself establish that property held by a family member is joint, and the burden of proving that an acquisition was made with joint family funds shifts only when an adequate income-producing nucleus is shown.
material_facts: The family possessed ancestral lands of about 56 acres, but their income was found insufficient even for the members’ maintenance.

The acquisitions and substantial house construction greatly exceeded the value of the ancestral lands’ contribution; the family’s ancestral lands remained intact and their income was used for maintenance.
The acquiring family member had long-term employment income and other resources.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not establish a sufficient nucleus to shift the initial burden; even assuming the burden shifted, the evidence established that the disputed purchases and buildings were self-acquisitions, not joint family property.
issues.legal_principle: Proof of a Hindu joint family does not raise a presumption that every member’s property is joint. The person asserting joint ownership must prove it. If the family has joint property which, by its nature and relative value, could have formed an adequate nucleus for the acquisition, the burden shifts to the person asserting self-acquisition to prove that the acquisition was made without its aid. The Court applied Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, which states this rule, and referred to Babubhai Girdharlal v. Ujamlal Hargovandas, Venkataramayya v. Seshamma and Vythianatha v. Varadaraja. The adequacy of the nucleus depends on the evidence, particularly its income and the scale and timing of the acquisitions.

rule.if: partition_claim and joint_family_exists and (nucleus_insufficient or (nucleus_adequate and self_acquisition_independently_proved))

predicates.partition_claim: A claimant seeks, in a partition proceeding, to treat property acquired or held by a family member as joint family property.
predicates.joint_family_exists: The parties belong to a Hindu joint family.
predicates.nucleus_insufficient: The family’s joint property could not, in light of its nature, income and relative value, reasonably have funded the acquisitions in dispute.
predicates.nucleus_adequate: The family’s joint property could, in light of its nature, income and relative value, reasonably have provided a foundation for the acquisitions in dispute.
predicates.self_acquisition_independently_proved: Evidence shows that the acquisitions were made without aid from joint family property, including that the joint property remained intact and its income was used for family maintenance.

issues.definition: When a partition claimant relies on joint family ownership, the acquisitions are not established as joint if the family lacked an adequate nucleus or, despite an adequate nucleus, independent evidence shows they were made without its aid.

issues.legal_issue: Relevant judgments tendered after the evidence has closed may be excluded for late production where admitting them would require reopening the trial and no basis for reopening is shown.
material_facts: The claimant tendered judgments from earlier maintenance proceedings after the hearing was about to commence.
Those judgments contained assertions that the disputed properties belonged to the joint family and were relevant to the extent of family property.
The documents were rejected as late, and admitting them after the evidence had closed would have required giving the opposing party an opportunity to adduce evidence and recommencing the trial.
issues.conclusion: The earlier judgments were relevant and admissible as assertions concerning rights under section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act, but their late production did not justify setting aside the rejection and reopening the case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Indian Evidence Act permits evidence of assertions concerning a right or custom in question; the earlier judgments qualified as such assertions. However, Order XIII, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure governed their late production. The Court held that the rejection should not be set aside where the documents were tendered after the evidence had closed and their admission would require the trial to be reopened.

rule.if: civil_trial and relevant_assertion_documents and documents_tendered_after_evidence_closed and admission_requires_reopening and no_basis_to_reopen

predicates.civil_trial: The documents are tendered in a civil trial.
predicates.relevant_assertion_documents: The documents contain assertions concerning a right or matter in question in the proceeding.
predicates.documents_tendered_after_evidence_closed: The documents are produced after the parties have closed their evidence.
predicates.admission_requires_reopening: Admitting the documents would require the opposing party to produce further evidence or the trial to recommence.
predicates.no_basis_to_reopen: No sufficient ground is shown to set aside the rejection and reopen the trial.

issues.definition: Relevant assertion documents tendered after evidence has closed remain excluded when their admission requires reopening the trial and no basis to reopen is shown.

issues.legal_issue: Property shown to have been possessed by a family from time immemorial may be presumed ancestral, placing on the party asserting self-acquisition the burden of proving it.
material_facts: The family had possessed several house plots for generations, and no title deeds showing their acquisition by an individual were produced.
The sanads for the plots recorded or confirmed prior occupation rather than proving a separate acquisition.
The evidence did not establish that the plots at issue had been acquired from the Government; a different plot was shown by a document to have been purchased at a Government auction.
issues.conclusion: The plots shown to have been in family possession from time immemorial were ancestral family property, and the claimant was entitled to a half share in their value; the separately proved Government-auction purchase was not subject to that claim.
issues.legal_principle: Although the party claiming joint property ordinarily bears the burden of proof, where property is shown to have been in a family’s possession from time immemorial, it is reasonable to presume that it is ancestral and to place the burden on the party pleading self-acquisition. The Court relied on this evidentiary principle and distinguished property for which acquisition by an individual was affirmatively established.

predicates.partition_claim: A claimant seeks a share of property in a partition proceeding.
predicates.family_possession_from_time_immemorial: The property is shown to have been possessed by the family for generations or from time immemorial.
predicates.no_individual_acquisition_proved: The party asserting separate ownership does not prove that a family member individually acquired the property.

issues.definition: In a partition claim, property possessed by the family from time immemorial, with no individual acquisition proved, is presumed ancestral and the claimant is entitled to a share.

issues.legal_issue: The relation-back doctrine for adoption applies to the adoptive father’s estate and does not permit an adopted son to divest an inheritance from a collateral that vested before the adoption.
material_facts: The claimant was validly adopted after the estate of a collateral had devolved by inheritance on another person.
The claimant sought to recover that estate by treating his adoption as relating back to the death of his adoptive father.
The disputed estate was inherited from a collateral, not part of the adoptive father’s estate.
issues.conclusion: The adopted son could not use the relation-back doctrine to divest the collateral estate that had vested by inheritance before his adoption.
issues.legal_principle: An adopted son acquires the rights of an aurasa son, and his adoption relates back to the adoptive father’s death, placing him in the position of a posthumous son with respect to the adoptive father’s estate. That fiction does not extend to a collateral’s estate: inheritance vests immediately in the nearest heir and cannot be divested by a later adoption. The Court relied on Bhubaneswari Debi v. Nilkomul Lahiri, Kally Prosonno Ghose v. Gocool Chunder Mitter and Nilkomul Lahuri v. Jotendro Mohan Lahuri, and dissented from Anant Bhikappa Patil (Minor) v. Shankar Ramchandra Patil insofar as it extended relation back to property inherited from collaterals. It also discussed Pratapsing Shivsing v. Agarsingji Raisingji, Amarendra Mansingh v. Sanatan Singh and Vijaysingji Chhatrasingji v. Shivasangji Bhimasangji as cases concerning the adoptive father’s estate, not collateral succession.

predicates.adoption_claim_to_collateral_estate: An adopted son claims property that belonged to a collateral rather than to his adoptive father.
predicates.collateral_inheritance_vested_before_ado: The collateral’s property had devolved by inheritance on an heir before the adoption occurred.

issues.definition: An adopted son cannot divest a collateral inheritance that vested in an heir before the adoption.

issues.legal_issue: A party asserting that separate property was blended into joint family property bears the burden of proving conduct showing an intention to abandon the separate claim.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that the collateral properties had been blended with the admitted ancestral properties.
The courts below concurrently found that the claimant had not proved that the defendants dealt with those properties in a manner showing an intention to abandon their separate claim.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to establish blending, and the collateral properties did not acquire the character of joint family property on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The burden of proving blending is heavily on the party asserting it. That party must establish that the owners dealt with the property in a way showing an intention to abandon their separate claim and impress it with the character of joint family property. The Court treated the issue as a question of fact and found no basis to disturb the concurrent findings below.

predicates.blending_claim: A party claims that separately held property was blended with joint family property.
predicates.no_conduct_showing_intention_to_abandon_: The party asserting blending does not prove conduct by the owners showing an intention to abandon their separate claim to the property.

issues.definition: A blending claim fails when the claimant does not prove conduct showing an intention to abandon the separate claim.
